newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Soros says single currency needed but flawed.
newsitem.headline: Soros says single currency needed but flawed.

text.p: Financier George Soros, who has made billions of dollars speculating on currencies, said on Saturday a single European currency was needed to stop such speculation but that its design as planned was flawed.

"The current exchange rate system is unstable because of trends following speculation," Soros told a weekend conference on European integration hosted by the Soros-financed Central European University.
"(But) the design of monetary union is flawed because in the long run you cannot have monetary union without a common fiscal policy and a central collection of taxes and redistribution," he said.
Soros said without such centralized mechanisms, parts of Europe could be in depression while the common monetary policy would not be able to counteract the situation.

Soros said measures to set up a central fiscal and tax collection system could be taken as a next step. But he warned that the political will for such a move might no longer be there after creation of a single currency because people might oppose further integration.
Lawmakers were already resentful of the accelerating process of what he called "social engineering."
"One has to recognise Europe is heading toward a crisis," he said, adding that the problem lay in undemocratic decision-making at the heart of Europe.
"The ultimate power is left with the individual national governments and what goes on in Brussels is a process of horse-trading among the national interests," he said.
"The common interest is not represented and the people feel increasingly alienated by the government which goes on in Brussels."
Soros suggested that as a result of this disenchantment, France could be the first member of the single currency plan to break ranks.
"One scenario would be a U-turn in France because the French are very restive due to the high level of unemployment which they blame with some justificaton on the move toward a common currency."
Soros said the only way to take people further down the road to integration was to increase the powers of their elected representatives in the European parliament.
"There is a need for the European parliament and the people to assert themselves," he told the conference.

Hungarian-born Soros has committed $200 million over 10 years to the Budapest-based university and after the end of communism set up the Open Society Foundation to promote democracy and freedom of information in emerging post-communist democracies.

The financier made close to $1 billion from a run on the pound in the weeks before Britain withdrew from Europe's currency grid in 1993 and was dubbed at the time "the man who broke the Bank of England."
